voiceover.text: A spectroscope spreads light out by wavelength. Inside, a grating or a prism sends each wavelength in a slightly different direction, and how a grating does that is a later video. Visible light is a tiny slice of the electromagnetic spectrum, from about four hundred nanometres for violet to about seven hundred for red. So a spectrum is a map. It shows how much light the source gives out at each wavelength.

Start with the filament. It's a coil of tungsten wire, heated by the current to about twenty-nine hundred kelvin. In a solid, the atoms are packed tightly and interact strongly, so their charges are shaken in every possible way. Remember, accelerating charges radiate. Shake them in every way, and you get every wavelength, with no gaps. That's a continuous spectrum. Heat the filament more, and it gets brighter, and its light shifts towards the blue end. But its smooth spread depends mainly on temperature, not on the metal, which is why it can't identify an element.

Now the discharge tube. It holds hydrogen gas at low pressure, with a high voltage across it. Electrons crash into the atoms and give them energy. Here's the key idea. An electron in an atom can only have certain energies, called energy levels. When it drops from a higher level to a lower one, the atom gives out light of one particular wavelength. A bigger drop gives a shorter wavelength. Hydrogen's drops down to the second level give its four bright visible lines, at six hundred and fifty-six, four hundred and eighty-six, four hundred and thirty-four, and four hundred and ten nanometres. In a thin gas the atoms are far apart, so each behaves on its own, and the lines stay sharp.

Every element has its own set of energy levels, so it has its own set of lines. That pattern is a fingerprint. Sodium gives two yellow lines, very close together, at five hundred and eighty-nine nanometres. Neon gives a crowd of red and orange lines. To identify a gas, match its lines to reference spectra, and every observed line has to match, not just one. Here's a surprise. In 1868, sunlight showed a yellow line that matched no element known on Earth. It was named helium, after the Greek word for the Sun, and it wasn't found on Earth for another twenty-seven years.

voiceover.text: Now put cool sodium vapour in front of the hot filament. Cool atoms sit in their lowest energy level. They absorb exactly the wavelengths they would give out, because the same energy gaps are involved, this time with electrons jumping up. So the rainbow comes through with two dark lines, at exactly the same places as sodium's bright yellow lines. The absorbed light isn't destroyed. It's given out again, but in all directions, so very little carries on towards you, and the line looks dark. The Sun works the same way. Its hot, dense layers give a continuous spectrum, and cooler gas above them absorbs, leaving the dark lines first mapped by Joseph von Fraunhofer.

What about sunlight bouncing off the Moon, a cloud or a sheet of white paper? You see the same dark lines, in the same places. Reflection doesn't make a new spectrum. The Moon isn't a glowing gas. It just sends sunlight back, so moonlight carries the Sun's pattern. That's also the safe way to look at sunlight. Never point a spectroscope at the Sun. Aim it at white paper or a cloud instead.

In the 1850s, Gustav Kirchhoff summed this up in three rules. Here's a way to remember them. Hot and dense, all colours. Hot and thin, bright lines. Cool and thin, in front of something hot, dark lines, in the same places.

In the investigation, you view each source through a spectroscope with a wavelength scale. A filament lamp, a few discharge tubes, and sunlight reflected from white paper.
